items.title: Louis James Interview, 1959-05-25
items.q: Yeah, my brothers. All four of you. Yeah, four of us. See, my four oldest brothers, a guitar player. Then my next brother next to me, he played trombone and clarinet and bass.

ctx.x: On the way home. Well, it happened that I wouldn't go to bed when you get back home by twelve, one o'clock, you know, on the excursion. And by knowing that song, by air, I said, well, let me read it before I go to bed, see. Yeah. So I just kept on, and that's why I know so much about music that I should know, because I learned how to read first sight, you see. Yeah. And then we'd have our rehearsal, you know, and put it down. See, I was so apt by heart, you know, well, I didn't need no music.
Well, these four brothers, were they the Gabriel brothers? No, no. Or your brothers?

Yeah, my brothers. All four of you. Yeah, four of us. See, my four oldest brothers, a guitar player. Then my next brother next to me, he played trombone and clarinet and bass. And my youngest brother in California now, he played saxophone, violin, and clarinet. And his son playing music too. Skeet, they call him. He played with the pijon.

items.title: Louis James Interview, 1959-05-25
items.q: I'd been knowing Manny, you know.

ctx.x: You must have been here quite a while, weren't you?
I said, no, it was 1915, I think. Oh. I came, yeah. And you went back? I went for Wooden Central Bank, you know. And that's why I'd been knowing Manny, you know. Yes.
Where did you work when you moved down in the district then? Where did you play there? At the Villa.
